title: Apache Phase-4 response body blocking bypass
description: In the Apache connector, response body buckets are now appended to libmodsecurity for inspection but are not retained by the connector. When a response brigade does not contain EOS, the filter immediately calls ap_pass_brigade() and sends the bytes onward. Phase-4 evaluation via msc_process_response_body() happens only later when EOS is seen. At that point, r->sent_bodyct may indicate that response data was already committed, causing the late-intervention resolver to choose log_only in the default safe mode. As a result, an attacker who can cause the protected upstream application to emit a response that is split across multiple brigades can receive content that a Phase-4 ModSecurity rule was configured to deny. This is a regression from the previous buffered design, which retained the response brigade until EOS and could deny before forwarding.

title: Privileged workflow executes updated submodule code
description: The workflow grants `contents: write` and `pull-requests: write`, checks out `master` with the default `actions/checkout` credential persistence, updates submodules from their remote tracking branches, and then executes `make quick-check`. In this repository, `quick-check` depends on `lint`, and `lint` executes Python and shell scripts from `modules/ModSecurity-test-Framework`, which is an external Git submodule. Because `git submodule update --remote --recursive` moves that submodule to the latest remote commit before validation, anyone who can compromise or push to the submodule upstream can cause arbitrary code in that submodule's `ci` scripts to run in this privileged scheduled workflow. That code can use the persisted checkout credentials or working tree to push branches, alter generated PR contents, or otherwise abuse the workflow's repository write permissions. The `continue-on-error: true` setting also means a PR is still created after the check fails, so malicious modifications made before failure may still be packaged for review.

title: Build guides now use unpinned, unverified source downloads
description: The new shared libmodsecurity guide makes the beginner/default path clone ModSecurity from GitHub without checking out a fixed tag, validating the resolved commit, verifying a tag, or running tests, then runs `sudo make install`. The NGINX guide similarly downloads an NGINX tarball without the previous signature verification and clones ModSecurity-nginx without pinning the release/commit. Before this commit, the connector guides used fixed refs, expected commit checks, and, for NGINX, release signature verification. This is a supply-chain hardening regression: users following the documented default path can build and install whatever the upstream default branch or downloaded artifact resolves to at that time. If an upstream repository, release distribution path, DNS/TLS trust path, or maintainer account is compromised, the documentation now steers users toward compiling and installing attacker-controlled WAF/connector code, potentially system-wide.

title: Blocking auth service can be slowloris-DoSed
description: The commit introduces common/runtime/http_authorization_service.c, used by the new Envoy ext_authz and Traefik forwardAuth starter services. The listener explicitly allows --listen 0.0.0.0:PORT, but after accept() the service processes the accepted socket inline and does not return to accept another connection until the full HTTP request, optional body, ModSecurity processing, and response write finish. Header and body reads use blocking recv() loops with no SO_RCVTIMEO, poll/select deadline, nonblocking mode, per-connection worker, or connection timeout. An attacker who can reach the service can connect and slowly drip an incomplete header, or declare a Content-Length within the configured body limit and never finish the body. That single connection blocks the entire authorization service. In a proxy deployment this can make legitimate requests hang or fail closed, causing an availability outage. The default smoke scripts use loopback, but the new CLI permits 0.0.0.0, making this remotely exploitable when operators expose the service.

title: Update workflow runs untrusted submodule code with write token
description: Before this patch, the workflow YAML was invalid because unquoted scalar values containing ': ' prevented parsing. The patch quotes those values, so the scheduled/manual workflow can now run. In the now-active workflow, the job grants contents:write and pull-requests:write, checks out master without disabling actions/checkout's default persisted credentials, updates submodules from their remote HEADs, and then runs make quick-check. That target depends on lint, which executes Python and shell scripts from the submodule path. The configured submodule is an external GitHub repository. A malicious or compromised maintainer of that submodule can place code in the framework scripts so that the next scheduled/manual update executes attacker-controlled code with the workflow's write-capable GitHub token available through persisted git credentials. continue-on-error does not mitigate this because the attacker code runs before the failure is handled. The safer pattern is to validate unreviewed dependency updates in a read-only job with persist-credentials:false, or avoid executing code from the newly updated submodule until after review; grant write permissions only to a separate PR-creation step/job that does not run untrusted code.

title: CI evidence gate bypassed by governance-only report check
description: This commit introduces a validation bypass in the generated-report security evidence gate. The strict `check-generated-report-layout` path still detects stale/blocked critical evidence and full-matrix critical runtime mismatches, but the new `report-governance` target calls the checker with `--governance-only`, which sets `strict_evidence` to false. In that mode, critical input freshness checks are skipped and `check_verified_runtime_diagnostics` returns immediately. The GitHub workflow now invokes only `make report-governance`, and `make lint` was also changed to invoke only `report-governance`, leaving the strict `verified-report-evidence-gate` target defined but not wired into the public workflow. I confirmed this behavior in the checked-out tree: the strict checker fails with `full-matrix critical mismatches detected: 764`, while the governance-only mode passes. This does not directly create a remote runtime exploit in the Apache/NGINX connectors, but it weakens a security-relevant CI gate intended to prevent merging with known critical WAF correctness evidence gaps.

title: Predictable /var/tmp verified-run root follows symlinks
description: The production Apache/NGINX connector runtime code was not changed. However, the commit introduces a local security issue in the verified-run/build harness path handling. The Makefile now defaults VERIFIED_RUN_ROOT to ${RUNNER_TEMP:-${TMPDIR:-/var/tmp}}/ModSecurity-conector-verified. The new runtime_path_utils helper has the same fixed /var/tmp fallback and deliberately no longer treats /var/tmp as a forbidden system write location. run-verified-report-run.py then calls Path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) and chmod(0755) on VERIFIED_RUN_ROOT and derived roots. These operations follow existing symlinks and do not verify owner, mode, or that the final resolved path is still a freshly-created private directory. On a multi-user host, an attacker can pre-create /var/tmp/ModSecurity-conector-verified as a symlink to an existing directory, or as an attacker-owned directory containing symlinks such as build, src, logs, or component-cache. If a more privileged user runs the verified tooling, the scripts may chmod the symlink target and later write build artifacts, logs, downloaded sources, or generated files under attacker-selected paths. At minimum this is a local denial-of-service/log redirection issue; when run as root it can alter permissions on sensitive directories and may expose or corrupt files. The safe pattern would be to use mkdtemp-style unpredictable roots or create the fixed root with O_NOFOLLOW/lstat ownership checks, reject symlinks, require the directory to be owned by the current user with safe permissions, and avoid chmoding paths resolved from attacker-writable parents.

title: CI blocked-status marker can be spoofed via child output
description: ci/tools/run-check-status.py classifies a child exit code 77 as an allowed blocked result when block_reason() finds exactly one approved CHECK_STATUS_REASON marker anywhere in the child's combined stdout and stderr. The wrapped Apache cleanup script emits diagnostic messages containing environment-controlled values such as FRAMEWORK_ROOT before exiting 77 for mandatory failures like a missing Framework. If such a value contains a newline followed by CHECK_STATUS_REASON apache_development_prerequisite, the runner treats that mandatory failure as the approved optional Apache development-prerequisite block and returns workflow success. This weakens CI integrity for the lint/quick-check path because the approval signal is parsed from unauthenticated mixed log output rather than a dedicated, non-injectable status channel.

title: Mixed Markdown fences bypass code-block parity check
description: The commit adds fenced_blocks() and uses it to require exact parity between English and German fenced code blocks. However, the parser treats any line starting with either ``` or ~~~ as both an opener and a closer. Markdown requires a closing fence to use the same marker character as the opening fence, with sufficient length. Because the checker does not remember the opening fence marker, a code block opened with ~~~ can be prematurely closed in the checker by a line starting with ```, even though that line is still content in rendered Markdown. Lines after that premature close are ignored by the checker until the real closing ~~~ is seen as a new unclosed block. As a result, English and German docs can contain different rendered code/configuration inside a fenced block while check_pairs_and_switches() reports no fenced-code-block mismatch. This does not affect connector runtime enforcement, but it weakens the new documentation-integrity control and could let security-sensitive translated examples diverge unnoticed.

title: Lighttpd Phase-4 deny can be applied after body is queued
description: In the patched lighttpd connector, Phase-4 response-body decisions are made at entity EOS. The new DENY_IF_POSSIBLE path treats the response as safely replaceable whenever headers/body are not yet committed to the socket, using write_queue.bytes_out as the only commit signal. However earlier response body chunks may already have been accepted into lighttpd's output queue before EOS. The new branch calls mod_msconnector_apply_decision() and returns PLUGIN_BODY_HOOK_ABORT without explicitly clearing any already-queued response bytes. This can produce an inconsistent/mixed response or allow malicious response bytes that triggered a Phase-4 rule to remain queued while the connector records a deny-style host action. The parent code explicitly avoided this by treating EOS-time Phase-4 disruption as safe log-only because body data might already be queued.

title: CI path policy can be bypassed via project roots
description: The new is_configured_project_path() exemption runs before the fixed system-prefix denylist. Because REPO_ROOT, CONNECTOR_ROOT, and FRAMEWORK_ROOT are environment/argument-derived values and are not validated to be narrow, non-system checkout paths, setting one of them to a sensitive parent such as /, /etc, or /root causes is_system_write_path() to return false for otherwise forbidden paths. allowed_runtime_roots() also appends these unvalidated roots, so is_allowed_runtime_path() can approve the same sensitive locations. prepare-runtime-components.py then installs the caller-supplied connector/framework roots into PATH_POLICY_ENV before checking cache/build/native roots, allowing cache/build paths under those forged roots to pass the system-write guard and be created/written by the runtime component preparation process. The previous implementation unconditionally classified /etc, /root, /usr, /var except /var/tmp, etc. as system write paths and also blocked paths inside source checkouts in readiness/report path checks.

title: Empty remote-rule override disables inherited rules
description: The new validation treats both NULL and empty strings as absent for remote-rule key/URL validation. However, the merge logic still treats any non-NULL child pointer as an explicit child override. As a result, if a parent has a complete remote rules pair and a child has rules_remote_key set to "" while rules_remote_url remains NULL, msconnector_config_merge() selects the child pair, msconnector_config_validate() now accepts it as no remote pair requested, and downstream rule loading skips the inherited remote rules. Before this commit, the same merged key-empty/url-NULL pair failed validation because the old check only compared NULL-ness. In deployments or future connectors that use this common config model with delegated child/location configuration, this can silently disable inherited remote WAF rules. The current Apache and NGINX runtime connectors appear to load remote rules directly rather than through this common helper, so this is not an unauthenticated HTTP-triggered runtime issue in the present production connectors.

title: Unbounded request-body reads in smoke harness
description: The commit adds POST/request-body handling to the local open-connector smoke harness. The new read_request_body() helper trusts Content-Length and chunk sizes and accumulates the entire body into memory with no maximum size or socket timeout. RuntimeDecisionHandler and the Lighttpd sidecar proxy call this helper before making an authorization decision, and the upstream test server also reads Content-Length bytes directly. Envoy and Traefik generated configs set a 4096-byte auth-body limit, but the Python auth server itself and the Lighttpd sidecar path do not enforce that limit. Because these servers bind only to 127.0.0.1 and run as development/CI smoke infrastructure, this is not a production WAF bypass, but a local same-host attacker during a smoke run could send a very large Content-Length or chunked request to consume memory, block handler threads, or fail the smoke job.

title: Unvalidated verified run id escapes build directory
description: This commit introduces verified-run orchestration that uses verified_run_id directly in filesystem paths without validating it as a safe filename segment or checking the resolved path remains under BUILD_ROOT/verified-runs. VERIFIED_RUN_ID can come from the environment, from BUILD_ROOT/verified-runs/current-run-id, or indirectly from the committed generated verified-run manifest via the Makefile. Values such as '../../outside' or absolute paths cause pathlib path joining to create directories and files outside the intended verified-runs tree. The primary writes are logs, verified-commands.json, and full-matrix temporary manifest/report directories. This is not a production WAF vulnerability and requires control of local CI/developer inputs or repository-generated report data plus execution of the new make targets, but it violates the repo's runtime-path containment expectations and can clobber/create files as the invoking user.

title: Strict evidence checker rejects BUILD_ROOT inputs
description: This commit adds strict validation of critical report input receipts, but the main check-generated-report-layout path calls check_manifest without passing a build_root. The validator does derive a default build root for its trusted root set, but it does not pass that derived value into resolve_input_reference. Since resolve_input_reference only expands BUILD_ROOT: references when a non-null build_root argument is provided, BUILD_ROOT: inputs generated by the report refresh manifest are treated as repository-relative paths such as <connector_root>/BUILD_ROOT:full-matrix/..., and are rejected as not trusted regular files even when the real file exists under the configured BUILD_ROOT. This is fail-closed and does not create a WAF/runtime security bypass, but it can break strict CI evidence validation after a valid full-matrix run.

title: Temporary report writers can clobber files via /tmp symlinks
description: Two repository-maintenance generators now default to `${TMP_ROOT:-/tmp}/modsecurity-doc-cleanup` and write deterministic report names with `Path.write_text()`. If a developer or maintainer runs either script without a private `TMP_ROOT`, a local attacker on the same machine can pre-create the predictable directory tree and place symlinks named like the generated outputs. The scripts accept existing directories via `mkdir(..., exist_ok=True)` and then follow symlinks while writing, allowing attacker-directed overwrite of files writable by the victim user. This does not affect the production Apache/NGINX/HAProxy request path, but it is a local developer/CI file-clobber issue in maintenance tooling. Use a private 0700 temporary directory, validate ownership/mode of existing directories, and open outputs with no-follow/exclusive semantics before writing.

title: HTX allow evidence accepts impossible transaction IDs
description: The commit adds safe_htx_transaction_id() and uses it to validate both the upstream-observed X-Request-Id and the transaction_id written to the allow event. The helper claims this is the grammar accepted by the native HTX filter, but it allows up to 256 characters. The actual native HTX overlay stores transaction IDs in char transaction_id[128] and rejects any candidate whose strlen() is greater than or equal to that buffer size. Therefore, an X-Request-Id between 128 and 256 safe characters can be forwarded upstream and logged by the harness, causing write_allow_event() to append an event with that long transaction_id even though the native HTX filter would not have used it as the libmodsecurity transaction ID and would have fallen back to HAProxy's stream unique ID. The default runtime script currently passes the short constant haproxy-htx-allow, so this is a harness evidence-integrity bug rather than an exploitable production issue.

title: German generated reports bypass layout checks
description: The new checks skip all `.generated.de.md` files before validating generated Markdown metadata, before detecting stale flat generated reports, and before detecting orphan/unregistered generated reports. This is too broad: a file such as `reports/testing/generated/evil.generated.de.md` is now accepted by `ci/check-generated-report-layout.py --governance-only` even though it is flat, unregistered, and has invalid generated-report metadata. This does not affect Apache/NGINX runtime request handling or WAF enforcement, so it is not a production security vulnerability, but it weakens CI/report governance and could hide stale or unintended translated report artifacts.

title: CI workflows reference invalid GitHub Action majors
description: No Apache/NGINX connector runtime code or production WAF logic was modified. The only observable issue is CI reliability: all workflows now depend on action references that are not the established current major versions changed from the previous commit. GitHub Actions resolves the `uses:` reference before the job can run; if the referenced tag does not exist, checkout/setup/artifact upload fails and the lint, scaffold, and smoke validation jobs do not execute. This is a CI availability/regression issue rather than a direct exploitable vulnerability in the connector.
